title: Executive Function Profiling
shortDescription: Planning, inhibition, working memory, and task-switching — the control processes behind goal-directed behavior.
longDescription: Executive Function Profiling is built on the scale structure of the BRIEF (Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function) — the clinical standard for self- and informant-rated executive function, widely used alongside performance-based tests. It measures eight control processes: Inhibit, Shift, Emotional Control, Initiate, Working Memory, Plan/Organize, Task Monitor, and Self-Monitor.
sourceNote: Original self-report items written to implement the BRIEF's published eight-scale structure (Inhibit, Shift, Emotional Control, Initiate, Working Memory, Plan/Organize, Task Monitor, Self-Monitor; the ninth scale, Organization of Materials, was left out as more about physical workspace tidiness than a distinct control process worth a digital self-report item) — the BRIEF itself (PAR Inc.) is a copyrighted, clinically normed, commercially administered instrument, so its actual items and norms are not reproduced here. Self-report inherently measures perceived executive function, not directly observed behavior the way a performance-based task (e.g. an N-back or Stroop) would — that's a real limitation of the self-report format itself, not specific to this adaptation.

resultRanges.title: Developing
resultRanges.description: Several control processes feel effortful right now — worth checking the eight scores above for which specific ones stand out most.
recommendations: Pick the single lowest-scoring scale above and focus on one concrete habit for it (e.g. a written task list for Plan/Organize)
External supports (timers, checklists, written reminders) compensate well for executive function gaps — use them deliberately, not as a last resort
Notice patterns across your day: executive function is often more fatigue-sensitive than other cognitive measures

resultRanges.title: Average
resultRanges.description: A typical mixed profile — some control processes stronger than others.
recommendations: Look at your two lowest scales above and build one small structural habit for each
Notice whether your weaker scales cluster (e.g. Inhibit + Emotional Control often move together) — that pattern is informative

resultRanges.title: Strong
resultRanges.description: Reliable executive control across most processes, with room to grow in one or two specific scales.
recommendations: Push your weakest scale specifically rather than practicing generically
Strong executive function compounds well with other cognitive strengths — check your Brain Profile for where it's paying off most

resultRanges.title: Very Strong
resultRanges.description: Consistently strong self-reported control across planning, inhibition, working memory, and task-switching.
recommendations: This level of executive control is a genuine asset in complex, multi-step, or high-distraction work
Consider whether your Self-Monitor score matches how others actually perceive you — it's worth checking that gap periodically

resultRanges.title: Exceptional
resultRanges.description: Uniformly strong across all eight executive function scales.
recommendations: This is a strong foundation for demanding, multi-threaded work — notice where it's already paying off
Since this is self-report, periodically sanity-check it against how consistently your actual follow-through matches your intentions

questions.questionText: I think before I act, even when I'm in a hurry.
I can stop myself from blurting out something I'll regret.
I stay in control of my reactions even when frustrated.
I adjust easily when plans change unexpectedly.
I can switch between tasks without losing my train of thought.
I handle changes to my daily routine without much trouble.
My emotional reactions tend to match the size of the situation, not bigger.
I recover quickly after something upsets me.
I stay calm even when things don't go my way.
I start tasks on my own without needing a push.
I get going on a project as soon as I've decided to do it.
I don't put off starting things I know I need to do.
I can hold several instructions in mind while completing a task.
I remember what I was doing after a brief interruption.
I keep track of multiple steps in a task without writing them down.
I break big tasks into manageable steps before starting.
I plan ahead rather than figuring things out as I go.
I organize my time well when I have multiple things to do.
I check my work for mistakes before considering it done.
I notice when I've gone off track partway through a task.
I review my progress periodically rather than only at the very end.
I notice how my behavior is affecting the people around me.
I can tell when I'm coming across differently than I intend to.
I adjust my approach when I sense it isn't landing well with someone.
